summary: Process explainer, not a single case. Built on NIJ, DOJ and FBI publications plus two contemporaneous news reports on the 2019 DOJ interim policy. A clearly labelled composite case is used to illustrate the steps; no real people are depicted.
timeline: July 2019: NIJ cold case best-practices guide
Sept 2019: DOJ interim policy on genetic genealogy approved
Nov 1 2019: DOJ interim policy takes effect

claims.claim: There is no single national definition of a cold case; agencies draw the line differently.
NIJ published National Best Practices for Implementing and Sustaining a Cold Case Investigation Unit in July 2019 with 23 recommendations in five categories.
CODIS began as a pilot software project in 1990.
The DNA Identification Act of 1994 formalized the FBI's authority to establish a national DNA index.
The National DNA Index System became operational in 1998.
Improved DNA methods can work with old, degraded or limited evidence; once-inconclusive samples may now yield profiles.
There is no consistent national policy for releasing body-worn camera footage; it varies with state law and agency policy.
claims.note: Specific state examples are described generically, not attributed to named states.

claims.claim: BJA maintains a body-worn camera toolkit that covers policy, including public release.
NIJ recommends operationally separate cold case units staffed by experienced investigators assigned exclusively, with access to forensic support.
CODIS profiles originate at the local level and flow to state and national levels.
Database hits often occur long after an investigation is initiated, so units must be ready to act quickly.
The DOJ interim policy on forensic genetic genealogy was approved in September 2019 and took effect November 1, 2019.
Under the DOJ policy, other available techniques including a CODIS search are expected to be exhausted before genetic genealogy is used.
The DOJ policy includes a section limiting the use of a genetic association as the basis for an arrest.
claims.note: Exact wording of that section not quoted; narration paraphrases conservatively.

claims.claim: Under UCR, an offense is cleared by arrest when at least one person is arrested, charged, and turned over to the court for prosecution.
Cleared by exceptional means applies when elements beyond law enforcement's control prevent an arrest and charge.
claims.note: Death of the offender is a commonly cited example.

claims.claim: Law enforcement use of genetic genealogy raises privacy concerns and is debated.
claims.note: Supporters cite solved violent crimes; critics cite consent and third-party privacy.

claims.claim: Montana and Maryland were the first states to regulate law enforcement use of forensic genealogy.
Maryland and the District of Columbia prohibit familial searching of their DNA databases.
The total number of cold cases in the United States.
claims.note: No single authoritative national count found; definitions and reporting differ.

claims.claim: The NIJ guide addresses victim-centered and trauma-informed approaches, media, and sustaining units beyond short-term funding.

disclaimers: This video describes general investigative and legal processes and is not legal advice.
The case used to illustrate the process is a composite; it is not a real case and depicts no real people.
